name: Oligopeptide-68

card.summary: A cosmetic peptide marketed as a tyrosinase inhibitor for brightening; human data are limited to small melasma studies of multi-ingredient products.
card.aka: Beautifeye (as listed in community notes); TGF-beta1 biomimetic oligopeptide-68
card.note: Studied only in combination formulas, so its individual contribution is not isolated.

quick.overview:
Oligopeptide-68 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide described in the literature as a TGF-beta1 biomimetic that inhibits the enzyme tyrosinase, which is involved in making melanin. It is sold as a skin-brightening ingredient in serums and creams.

The available human research consists of two melasma studies in which it was one component of a multi-ingredient regimen, so what it does on its own has not been separated out.
quick.mechanism: According to the study authors, oligopeptide-68 inhibits tyrosinase activity, the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis [1]. In one study it was paired with diacetyl boldine, which is described as stabilizing tyrosinase in its inactive form [1].
quick.risks: The studies reviewed here were of combination products that also contained exfoliating acids, sunscreen filters or other depigmenting agents, so adverse effects cannot be attributed to the peptide alone. It is a cosmetic ingredient in the US and EU rather than a drug.

lead: Oligopeptide-68 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide marketed as a skin-brightening ingredient. In the dermatology literature it is described as a TGF-beta1 biomimetic oligopeptide that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production [1]. People use products containing it to even out dark patches and give the complexion a brighter, more uniform tone.

Interest centres on facial hyperpigmentation, especially melasma, which Wikipedia describes as tan, brown or greyish patches, most often on the cheeks, nose, upper lip, forehead and chin, triggered by sun, hormones and genetics and prone to relapse [3]. Standard treatments named there include hydroquinone, tretinoin, azelaic acid and strict sun protection [3].
Published human evidence consists of two studies in which oligopeptide-68 was one component of multi-ingredient melasma regimens [1][2].

chain: Peptide inhibits tyrosinase in melanin production
Less pigment forms in dark patches
angle.text: Oligopeptide-68 is used in brightening serums and creams by people with melasma or uneven pigmentation who want a more even complexion. Studies so far test it inside combination formulas with sunscreen and exfoliating agents.

paras: Oligopeptide-68 appears in brightening and depigmenting cosmetic products aimed at facial hyperpigmentation such as melasma [1][2].

The authors of a 2016 melasma study describe oligopeptide-68 as inhibiting tyrosinase activity, whereas the co-formulated diacetyl boldine stabilises tyrosinase in an inactive form [1]. Hydroquinone, the long-standing comparator, also works by inhibiting tyrosinase [3].

A randomized, double-blind 12-week study of 40 women (38 completed) in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology tested two formulations, one with diacetyl boldine and one with oligopeptide-68, used together with other hypopigmenting or exfoliating agents and sunscreen for facial melasma. Melasma scores improved at weeks 6 and 12 versus baseline, most participants had only temporary mild skin reactions, and about 76% rated themselves moderately improved. The formulations were also compared with 2% and 4% hydroquinone on sun-protected skin of the arms, and the title reports each was equal to or better than 4% hydroquinone there [1].

A 2020 study of 20 women aged 29 to 61 used reflectance confocal microscopy to assess a complex of oligopeptide-68, phytic acid, glycolic acid, lactic acid and octinoxate over three months and reported significant improvement clinically and at cellular level without adverse reactions [2]. Because both studies tested combinations, they do not isolate the contribution of oligopeptide-68 itself.
Wikipedia notes melasma is chronic and relapsing, that sun exposure can bring it back after fading, and that broad-spectrum sunscreen with physical blockers is preferred [3].

timeline.event: Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology study of oligopeptide-68 and diacetyl boldine formulations in melasma [1].
Reflectance confocal microscopy study of an oligopeptide-68-based complex in melasma [2].

refs.title: Combined use of two formulations containing diacetyl boldine, TGF-β1 biomimetic oligopeptide-68 with other hypopigmenting/exfoliating agents and sunscreen provides effective and convenient treatment for facial melasma.
